tldr: We propose "CRS", an evaluation metric that diagnoses forced motions that ignore joint mechanics—something invisible to 1-bit binary success metrics—by projecting commanded velocities onto the joint axis to separate "progress" from "waste".
overview:
When robots manipulate articulated objects like doors and drawers (mechanisms with hinges or rails), most benchmarks evaluate them purely on binary task success (whether they managed to open it or not). However, this evaluation method has a major pitfall. Even when a task succeeds, conventional metrics cannot detect whether the robot commanded unnatural, forced motions that ignore the object's joint mechanics. For instance, if a policy trained on door opening/closing is applied to a drawer, it pulls forcefully in a circular arc like a door, yet is judged as a "success" more than half the time.

To solve this, the authors propose "Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS)," an evaluation metric that references the object's kinematic constraints directly. Assuming a secure grasp, it projects the robot end-effector's commanded velocity (twist) onto the object's joint axis. This decomposes the motion into two channels for evaluation: "progress velocity," which acts to properly open the joint, and "waste," which represents off-constraint rotations that the mechanism does not permit. This method requires neither recorded expert demonstration trajectories nor a separately learned judge model.

In experiments on 74 simulated articulated objects (doors, drawers, faucets) within the ManiSkill simulator, the authors showed that while standard success rates lumped three transfer failures together as mere performance drops, CRS gave each failure a distinct signature, attributing the exact cause. Furthermore, CRS demonstrated practical robustness, with verdicts remaining stable even with joint-axis estimation errors of up to 30 degrees.
contributions: Proposed "CRS", an evaluation metric that assesses the validity of robot command gestures using only a joint-axis model, without any recorded demonstrations or learned judges.
Quantified motion quality by decomposing commanded end-effector twist into two channels: "progress along the joint" and off-constraint "waste rotation".
Introduced "Matched Faithfulness Gates" that match commanded values against one-step physical displacement to ensure the physical consistency of the commands.
Exposed "false-passes" where a door-trained policy inappropriately opened drawers, demonstrating clear diagnosis of failure modes indistinguishable by standard success rates.

sections.heading: Why is evaluating solely on "success or failure" not enough?
sections.summary: "Task success rate", the dominant metric in robot manipulation evaluation, aggregates perception, grasping, and policy into a single bit, making it impossible to diagnose failure causes while overlooking successes achieved through incorrect motions. Because existing detailed metrics require expensive demonstration data or per-task stage definitions, we propose "CRS", which evaluates commanded gestures directly by referencing the kinematic constraints of the object itself.
sections.details:
Evaluation of robot manipulation policies has long relied on binary metrics: did the task succeed or fail (1 or 0)? However, that single bit of information compresses perception, grasp acquisition, execution, and control strategy into one number. As a result, two policies failing for completely different reasons end up with the same "0" score, while a policy executing completely wrong gestures can erroneously receive a passing "1".

Particularly hazardous is "apparent success." For example, when a Behavior Cloning (BC) policy trained on opening doors is applied to a drawer, it commands door-like arcing rotational motions that completely ignore the drawer's rails. Despite this, it succeeds in opening the drawer in 59 out of 110 episodes, yielding a passing success rate. In real-world articulated object manipulation, such unnatural commands that fight kinematics cause severe wear or breakage to the robot's arm and the object.

Of course, richer evaluation metrics have been proposed. However, measuring distance to demonstration trajectories requires recording data for every object, sub-goal evaluation requires hand-crafting phase definitions for every task, and learned judges require training dedicated evaluation models. These approaches do not scale to benchmarks spanning massive numbers of tasks and objects.

Prior work like MetaFine conducts geometric checks on actions and measures trajectory stability. However, its geometric tests are limited to tolerance-gated pass/fail verdicts, and its stability score lacks an object model. Thus, it cannot quantify—as a signed, continuous metric—how much of a command makes progress along the joint versus how much is wasted fighting the constraint.

Mechanically, the movable part of an articulated object can only move along its rails or hinges. Therefore, the signatures of improper, constraint-violating gestures do not appear in the resulting moved trajectory; they only manifest in the robot's command values and internal reaction forces. This study introduces "Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS)," which takes the object's 1-DoF screw axis kinematics as the reference and evaluates policies by projecting the commanded end-effector twist onto it.

sections.heading: How CRS separates "progress" from "waste" via joint-axis projection
sections.summary: CRS computes "progress velocity along the joint" and "waste rotation fighting the constraint" by projecting the policy's commanded end-effector velocity onto the object's joint axis in post-grasp reference states. Furthermore, it ensures evaluation reliability by establishing a one-step physical gate to verify whether the command actually produces the intended displacement in simulation.
sections.details:
To isolate confounding factors such as perception and grasp acquisition, CRS evaluates policies in counterfactual reference states where the handle is already held in a valid grasp. A scripted oracle (expert controller) guides the robot along a sequence of states that open the object, and CRS probes what end-effector commands the target policy outputs at each of these states.

### Decomposing the command
In the robot base frame, let the end-effector twist (spatial velocity) commanded by the policy at grasp point $c \in \mathbb{R}^3$ be $\mathcal{V} = [\omega^\top, v^\top]^\top \in \mathbb{R}^6$, where $\omega$ is angular velocity and $v$ is linear velocity. The object's joint constraint is defined by a unit direction vector $\hat{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ (and for revolute joints, an axis point $o \in \mathbb{R}^3$).

Based on this geometry, CRS decomposes the command as follows:
- **Progress along a revolute joint**: Computes the component of end-effector rotation around the joint axis: $\dot{q}_\omega = \omega^\top \hat{n}$ (rad/s).
- **Progress along a prismatic joint**: Computes the component of end-effector translation along the joint axis: $\dot{q}_{\mathrm{pris}} = v^\top \hat{n}$ (m/s).
- **Waste rotation**: Computes the rotational component not admitted by the joint: $\eta_\omega = \|\omega - (\omega^\top \hat{n})\hat{n}\|$ (rad/s). For prismatic joints, since no rotation is admitted, this is simply $\eta_\omega = \|\omega\|$.

A key strength is that these channels used for verdicts require only the axis orientation $\hat{n}$. For revolute joints, an estimated velocity $\dot{q}_v$ derived from the tangential component of linear velocity is also computed for supplementary diagnosis.

### Matched faithfulness gates
Evaluating raw commands is only meaningful if they correspond to real physics. Therefore, CRS introduces "faithfulness gates" that step the simulator forward by one step from the reference state using the commanded action, comparing the realized joint displacement $\Delta q_{\mathrm{real}}$ with the commanded velocity $\dot{q}\Delta t$.

Specifically, it verifies magnitude consistency using the coefficient of determination $R^2$ from linear regression between commands and displacements, and checks whether the sign (direction) matches for displacements exceeding the 95th percentile of at-rest sensor noise. Furthermore, an "equivalence band" set within $\pm 5\%$ of the oracle velocity allows small unintended motions to be cleanly evaluated as zero.

sections.heading: Uncovering "false passes" from wrong gestures and diverse failure modes
sections.summary: Using 74 articulated objects in ManiSkill, we rigorously examined transfer behaviors when applying a door policy to drawers and faucets using CRS. As a result, we detected 40 times the waste rotation on drawers that binary success rates missed, and demonstrated that distinct failure modes—such as counter-productive pushing or off-axis motions—can be clearly classified and attributed.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
Experiments were conducted in ManiSkill across 74 articulated objects from three GAPartNet categories (39 doors, 22 drawers, 13 faucets). The evaluated policies included OpenVLA-7B (fine-tuned with LoRA) and a point-cloud-based Behavior Cloning (BC) policy trained from scratch, evaluated in a leave-one-mechanism-out transfer setting.

### Validator Sanity Checks
When executing oracle commands, commanded velocities and one-step realized displacements showed high determination coefficients (doors: $R^2=0.69$, drawers: $0.89$, faucets: $0.65$), with direction concordance reaching 1.000 (perfect agreement) above the noise floor. In control experiments applying a drawer-only policy to doors, rotation around the door axis was nearly zero (less than 1/12.9th of the equivalence band), validating the instrument's accuracy.

### Detecting False-Passes from Wrong Gestures
When the door-trained BC policy was applied to drawers, it achieved task success in 59 out of 110 episodes (across 20 of 22 drawers). Standard success rates would interpret this merely as "a minor drop from 0.77 to 0.54." However, CRS revealed that in these successful episodes, the policy commanded an astonishing $1.27$ rad/s of off-axis rotation (waste rotation $\eta_\omega$). Compared to the passes of a drawer-trained policy ($0.032$ rad/s), it was exerting roughly 40 times the waste rotational torque. This waste rotation was virtually identical between pass and fail episodes ($1.27$ vs. $1.26$ rad/s), proving it is a persistent characteristic of the policy's gesture rather than an outcome artifact.

### Detecting Counter-Productive Pushing and Off-Axis Gestures
With the same door-trained models, applying OpenVLA to drawers resulted in counter-productive commands in the "closing" direction (negative velocity). Because the drawer was already closed, it did not move in one step, making realized displacement $\Delta q_{\mathrm{real}}$ look like a simple stop. While binary success rate merely logs this as a generic "failure", CRS's signed progress velocity captured the negative value, identifying that it was attempting to push closed.

When transferred to faucets (off-axis), hand translation accidentally turned the faucet to some extent, yielding realized displacements reaching 68% of the oracle. However, CRS's waste rotation channel flagged an anomalous value 5.4 times that of the oracle. By pairing signed progress velocity with waste rotation, CRS cleanly separated counter-productive pushes, off-axis motions, and false passes into distinct diagnostic cells that prior metrics conflated.

### Robustness to Joint Model Errors
In real robots, perfect joint axis models are unavailable. We therefore tested robustness by injecting noise: axis tilts up to 30 degrees and position offsets up to 5 cm. Evaluated relative to an oracle scored with the same axis, CRS qualitative verdicts remained completely unchanged under axis errors up to 30 degrees. Absolute thresholds tolerated axis tilt errors up to roughly 8 degrees.

sections.heading: Summary and future prospects toward real-world deployment
sections.summary: Using only joint axis information, CRS is a powerful evaluation tool that attributes the causes of failures invisible to success rates and exposes false passes achieved through unnatural gestures. While currently limited by assumptions like single 1-DoF joints and rigid grasps, it holds strong potential when paired with real-world RGB-D axis estimation and proprioception.
sections.details:
CRS interprets robot command gestures against explicit kinematic constraints: the object's joint axes. This enables it to pinpoint the root causes of failures that traditional success rates detect but cannot explain, bringing to light apparent successes achieved through mechanically impermissible motions. Because it operates without demonstration data as long as joint axes are defined, it serves as an extremely useful framework to complement existing manipulation benchmarks such as MetaFine.

### Limitations of this work
The authors highlight several assumptions and limitations:
- **Rigid Grasp Assumption**: It assumes the end-effector and handle are rigidly fixed together. However, as seen when translation coupled into joint motion in faucet experiments, real grasps can slip or have compliance.
- **Mechanism Scope**: The current formulation is tailored to single 1-DoF joints (revolute or prismatic) and only uses angular waste ($\eta_\omega$) in the scored metric.
- **Command-Based Evaluation**: Waste is evaluated purely from the robot's command values; it does not measure the actual physical cost (joint overload or hardware wear) inflicted in the real world.

### Future Outlook
Future extensions plan to support other lower pairs, such as helical, cylindrical, and planar joints. For real-robot deployment, estimating joint axes online from RGB-D cameras and reading realized displacements from the robot's proprioception could enable constraint-referenced debugging and evaluation in physical environments.

takeaways: Even with a 100% task success rate, "false passes" exist where robots command forced motions violating joint mechanics; geometric checks at the command level are essential.

By simply projecting the end-effector twist into two channels—progress along the joint axis and orthogonal waste rotation—motion quality can be quantitatively diagnosed without demonstrations or learned judges.
When a task fails, combining signed progress velocity and waste components automatically diagnoses whether the robot is pushing in reverse, pulling off-axis, or simply outputting insufficient effort.
limitations: Assumes a rigid grasp where the gripper and handle are locked together; slip or compliance at the grasp can break the correspondence between commands and resulting motion.
Currently formulated only for single 1-DoF revolute and prismatic joints, meaning it cannot be directly applied to multi-DoF, spherical, or compliant/deformable constraints.
Primarily validated in simulation; it does not measure the actual physical damage or stress inflicted on real-world hardware (motors and gearboxes) by wasteful commands.
